newsitem.title: USA: Georgia indicators predict surprising strength.
newsitem.headline: Georgia indicators predict surprising strength.

text.p: ATLANTA, Feb 3 - Georgia's Composite Index of leading indicators moved sharply higher in December, signaling that the state's 1997 economy may gain new momentum in the spring, state Labor Commissioner David Poythress said Monday.
Leading indicators rose 1.66 points in December to 146.12 on a 1988 index bases of 100. The index is designed to forecast economic activity three to six months ahead.
The Composite Index of Coincident Indicators, designed to measure current conditions, declined 0.04 points over the month to 146.05 on a 1987 base of 100.

Previous forecasts predicted Georgia's economy, which has slowed somewhat following the 1996 Summer Olympic Games, would continue to grow through 1997 but at a moderate pace. The December index of leading indicators could be a first signal that unanticipated new momentum is building, Poythress said.
The movement was fueled by increases in the number of new residential building permits, new motor vehicle sales and the average length of the manufacturing work week.
Although the numbers for new and continued unemployment claims were up for the month, total nonfarm employment held steady at 3.57 million, unchanged from November.
Residential building permits rose to 6,725 in December, a 12.08 percent increase over November's 6,000. The number of permits had fallen during each of the three previous months.

The average manufacturing workweek increased by 18 minutes in December, to 42.6 hours. That was an indication that total manufacturing employment, which grew by 500 to 590,000 in December, may rise at a more dramatic rate in January, Poythress said.
The state issued 42,294 titles for new motor vehicles in December, an increase of 1,139 or 2.77 percent over November.
Initial unemployment claims increased to 31,639 in December from 28,496 in November. But that was down sharply from 34,378 for December of last year.
Continued unemployment claims rose to 188,822 in December from 165,052 in November.

State revenue collections increased slightly in December, rising 0.02 percent to $861 million, despite the continuing lag in sales tax collections that resulted in the Oct. 1, reduction in the levy on groceries.
Average weekly manufacturing earnings rose by $6.30 in December to $480.98, due in part to increasing overtime hours. The figure was been four percent lower at $462.49 a year ago.
The state's unemployment rate held steady at 4.6 percent in December, unchanged from November.
